Issued at 145 PM CDT Sun Sep 6 2026

Other than enhanced 250 mb winds on the leading edge of the Pacific 
Northwest trough, 12Z upper-air observations show that the overall 
synoptic pattern is mostly unchanged with the Omega-block still 
clearly evident. However, beginning this afternoon and evening, the 
thermal ridge will begin to erode as the region of enhanced winds 
continues to intensify into a 120+ kt jet streak over the 
Intermountain West on the upwind side of the ridge. This will 
provide sufficient energy and momentum for the stagnant Pacific 
Northwest trough to carried eastward, ultimately deamplifying the 
ridge. Although it will be a days-long process, this transition is 
high confidence with both the HREF and LREF 10th to 90th percentile 
spreads showing a height difference of only about 1-3 dam through 
Tuesday with the ridge being fully suppressed by Wednesday. 

Overnight Saturday into Sunday, a backdoor cold front moved through 
much of the CWA; latest observations and surface analysis suggest 
that this boundary has stalled just west of the MO/KS border. 
Temperatures are expected to top out in upper 80s/low 90s across 
northern MO today behind that boundary. Further south where the 
Extreme Heat Warning remains in effect, temperatures are anticipated 
to be similar to yesterday in the mid/upper 90s and heat index 
values around 105F or greater. 

As we head into the afternoon and evening hours tonight, the 
evolution of the environment will need to be monitored closely. 
Compared to the previous forecast cycle, the likelihood of storm 
development in the afternoon has increased (now 30-50% chance 
generally along and west of the I-35 corridor). Cloud cover 
associated with weak convection and showers to our north and west 
have struggled to make it into Missouri. With abundant sunshine and 
solar heating, considerable destabilization is underway. By late 
afternoon, we could see up to 3500 J/kg MLCAPE and an eroding 850mb 
warm nose. Additionally, an outflow boundary from decaying showers 
in central Kansas has been noted throughout much of the late morning 
hours from KTWX. Depending on how far east this outflow progresses, 
it could be a focal point for storm development this evening. For 
what it's worth, the most recent runs of the CAMs do appear to be 
initiating convection in a comparatively more organized manner 
compared to the disorganized clusters noted in earlier runs which 
does suggest some boundary interactions. SPC has maintained the 
Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) for severe weather in our area this 
afternoon and evening with the main threats being hail and damaging 
winds. The severe threat appears greatest during daylight hours 
today when buoyancy is better for lofting hailstones and sub-cloud 
layer profiles are more suggestive of downburst wind potential.
Forecast PWATs are also near the top of climatology around 1.9" to 
2.1" so isolated pockets of heavy rainfall will also be possible. 
WPC has a Slight Risk (Level 2 of 4) of excessive rainfall in 
northwestern Missouri today and tonight. After sunset, expect a 
general downtrend in the severe threat with any ongoing storms 
though the hydro threat may continue with additional showers/storms 
moving into the area, mainly in northwest Missouri. 

More uncertainty exists with the late evening and overnight 
potential for showers and storms as it is more dependent on factors 
across the Northern Plains where convection has been ongoing for 
much of the morning and early afternoon. A shortwave helping sustain 
this activity will continue eastward tonight which may encourage 
continued development. Notably, the steering flow shrouding this 
shortwave has a strong northerly component that could draw storms 
into northern Missouri sometime after dark (roughly a 20-40% 
chance). There would be a much lesser severe threat with these 
storms, but heavy downpours and some gusty winds would still be 
possible. Showers/storms should weaken and decay with time, but some 
may linger through early Monday morning.

Areas across northern Missouri can also expect "cooler" high 
temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s once again on Monday, with 
areas between the US-36 and I-70 corridors in the low/mid 90s. South 
of I-70 and near the MO/KS border, temperatures are expected to 
remain in the mid/upper 90s. The Extreme Heat Warning continues for 
the Kansas City Metro and south until 8 PM on Tuesday where there is 
higher confidence in 105F heat index values. Additional heat 
headlines may need to be considered for portions of central Missouri 
on Tuesday and Wednesday but will defer to future forecast cycles as 
the timing of a midweek cold front remains unclear. Currently, the 
most likely timeframe for the front to move through looks to be 
overnight Tuesday into early Wednesday. If this holds true, a 
headline on Wednesday would probably be unnecessary but a headline 
may still be warranted in central MO on Tuesday. By Thursd
